Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PA View image in fullscreen Clifford Wilby, who also filmed the MP on his mobile phone, was found guilty of using threatening, abusive, or insulting words or behaviour to cause harassment, alarm, or distress. Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PA Crime ‘Abusive’ man found guilty of harassing Stella Creasy MP on tube train Clifford Wilby, 63, blocked the Walthamstow MP from leaving, filmed her and talked about her ‘failings as a member of parliament’ Nadeem Badshah Tue 11 Aug 2026 13.46 EDT First published on Tue 11 Aug 2026 13.28 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A 63-year-old man has been found guilty of harassing the Labour MP Stella Creasy after he was “abusive and aggressive” to her on a tube train. Clifford Wilby, of east London , saw the MP for Walthamstow in July 2025 on a Victoria Line train, Westminster magistrates court heard. He blocked her from leaving the tube carriage and started talking to her about knife crime and her “failings as a member of parliament” and then filmed her on his mobile phone, the court heard. Other passengers intervened and got in between them before Creasy left the carriage. Sarah Madden, prosecuting, said the pair first met during a Zoom meeting in 2024 in Creasy’s capacity as an MP. The meeting was terminated due to Wilby’s behaviour. Creasy, giving evidence from behind a screen, said during the online meeting he “made a series of very serious allegations”, became abusive and “referred to the fact he had been diagnosed as a psychopath”. She said he started to make a complaint about a constituent and she reminded him that she could not discuss somebody else’s case. He became “abusive, aggressive” and they terminated the conversation, said Creasy. View image in fullscreen Stella Creasy, the Labour MP for Walthamstow. Photograph: Nicola Tree Creasy said that on 15 July last year she had boarded a Victoria line train and was intending to move further down the train at the next stop, and looked up to get off the train and made eye contact with the defendant. “He said ‘are you Stella Creasy?’, at that point my memory kicked in and I made the connection because I knew his face, he then confirmed he was Clifford Wilby,” said the MP. “He stood up and blocked my ability to leave the carriage, he began talking to me about his concerns about my constituent, he was shouting although the tube train is a loud environment.” She added: “Obviously I was concerned that I was in an enclosed space with him. He was very close. “I stated very clearly this wasn’t an appropriate conversation to be having.” Creasy said at this point she was backed up against the door of the carriage and was holding her hands out as a gesture “to say stop”. She got off the train at Finsbury Park by exiting through another door further up the carriage. Tess McCarthy, defending, put to the MP that she could have got off the train as the incident continued to which Creasy replied “no”. Wilby said he had been hoping to continue the conversation about the constituent on the tube but the MP “became quite agitated” and he was “quite shocked by her reaction”, so he pressed record on his phone “for my safety”. He added: “At no point did I stand in front of her. When I first spoke to her she was actually getting off the train and she turned around to speak to me, I stood up because it was noisy.” The defendant also denied telling Creasy in 2024 he had been diagnosed as a psychopath. The deputy chief magistrate Tan Ikram found Wilby guilty of using threatening, abusive, or insulting words or behaviour to cause harassment, alarm, or distress and adjourned sentencing until 8 September for reports. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8en.text: Image source, Courtesy of Audrey and Arthur Kermalvezen Image caption, Audrey and Arthur Kermalvezen met at a gathering of donor-conceived activists Published 30 August 2026, 00:03 BST For years, Arthur Kermalvezen, the child of a sperm donor, saw possible fathers everywhere he went. "I imagined it might be my teacher, the people I saw on the bus... and I was very angry because it's impossible to live like this." When, as an adult, he fell in love with Audrey, another sperm donor baby from Paris, the question became even more pressing. Audrey describes the moment they met at a gathering for donor conceived activists in 2010 as "love at first sight" - but was this connection a romantic or genetic attraction? When they were born, there were only two sperm banks in Paris and many men had made multiple donations - so there was a real possibility they could be half-siblings. Before building a life together, Arthur and Audrey needed to know whether they were related. But in France, laws governing genetic testing and donor anonymity made finding the answer extremely difficult. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, It is a criminal offence to take a home DNA test in France In France, only a research scientist, doctor or judge can order and supervise a genetic test, and people can be fined more than â¬3,500 ($4,288; Â£3,191) for possessing a home testing kit. As a result, companies such as 23andMe, Ancestry and MyHeritage don't make their kits available in France. Supporters of the law, in place since 1994, say it stops sensitive genetic data being given to commercial companies, and prevents family disputes being caused by unexpected results. But Arthur points out that France is the only country in Europe that criminalises the use of such tests. Immediate chemistry Even before her parents told her as an adult that she was donor-conceived, Audrey had qualified as a lawyer, specialising in bioethics law. Because of this, she fully understood that French law had guaranteed donor anonymity, even after a donor's death. But Audrey had been conceived in 1979, before any such legislation existed. Image source, Courtesy of Audrey and Arthur Kermalvezen Image caption, Audrey and Arthur have both campaigned for the right to know one's origins While searching for other donor-conceived people born before 1994, Audrey came across Arthur. He had written a book detailing his desire to learn more about his biological origins. Audrey says she was struck by how precisely he expressed feelings she herself had struggled to articulate. Both had loving families, yet both found themselves drawn to questions about the unknown people who had helped to create them. When they met in person the chemistry was immediate. So was the problem. Before they could move from platonic friendship to a romantic relationship, and even build a life together, they had to know the truth about their fathers. But no one in authority was willing to tell them. In search of the truth After months of searching, they found a doctor in southern France who, for â¬900 ($1,028; Â£764) in cash, conducted a genetic test which found that they were not related. But their unease remained as the doctor was breaking the law in sharing that result with them. "We were worried he was a charlatan," Audrey says. They considered using a home-testing kit to confirm the result, but as a lawyer, Audrey was determined to act within the law. So, from 2010, she launched a series of legal challenges to the French system. She wanted to know whether her donor was still alive and, if so, whether he still wished to remain anonymous. Could she access non-identifying information about how many times he had donated and whether Arthur could be among her half-siblings? Her efforts failed. After three years of legal challenges, the couple took a 'leap of faith' and got married. In 2015, France's highest administrative court rejected Audrey's final appeal. Image source, Courtesy of Audrey Kermalvezen Image caption, In 2013, they took a leap of faith and got married Shortly before the birth of their first child, a doctor agreed to investigate what information might exist about their respective donors. Under French law, a medical practitioner has access to this information about their patients, but is not allowed to share it with them. The doctor found that their donors were born in different years - and so could not be the same man. A life-changing piece of information, but one they only gained because a doctor agreed to break the rules. "It's completely weird," Audrey says, "because it means that the doctor can know more than me... about me." Even with this new information, Arthur still worried they could be related, so after years of resisting it, they finally took a home DNA test. Campaigners say the French ban has done little to stop people taking home tests, with the advocacy group DNA Pass estimating that well over a million French people have taken one. Many order them via friends in countries where they are legally obtainable - or by using forwarding services in neighbouring countries. The test said they weren't related. DNA shock The DNA results soon opened more doors. After 30 years of imagining who his father might be, Arthur finally made contact with his sperm donor on Christmas Day in 2017. But Audrey had the greatest shock. Among her DNA matches was a woman named Sophie whom she'd represented in court. The two women had been fighting for similar legal rights. "I discovered that Sophie - a woman whose case I had pleaded in court - was my biological sister," Audrey says. Image source, Courtesy of Audrey Kermalvezen Image caption, Arthur and Audrey finally built their family Audrey and Arthur had taken their DNA test alongside eight other donor-conceived activists campaigning for access to their origins. Of the 10, four turned out to share the same donor: Audrey, her brother Peter, Sophie and Sophie's brother David - highlighting how real the risk of a shared donor had always been. Image source, Courtesy of Audrey and Arthur Image caption, Today, Audrey and Arthur have three children together Many years later, a genetic match with an American led Audrey to her donor - a man called Philippe - but he had already died. Audrey's mother wrote Philippe's family a letter, thanking them for his "gift" which she described as "immeasurable". His family welcomed Audrey for a visit. "Everybody had tears in their eyes," recalls Audrey. Philippe's sister had never known he was a donor. The discovery gave Audrey answers that she had sought for decades. She learned details about her biological family's medical history. She saw photographs and video footage of Philippe. "I can watch him, see how he moved and hear his voice." Audrey's legal campaign and Arthur's book together helped drive changes to French donor-conception laws, allowing people conceived after April 2025 to access identifying information about their donors when they reach adulthood. For now, however, France remains one of the few countries in Europe where at-home DNA testing is still prohibited. Which means, for Audrey, the wider fight continues. "Every person has the right to know their origins and the right to know their history," she says. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/08/12-n.text: The UK and France were among 12 countries to announce new trade sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank on Tuesday, amid what they called a "rapidly deteriorating" situation marked by increasing settler attacks on Palestinians.Canada, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden joined the UK and France in confirming plans to introduce restrictions on trade with settlements, according to a joint statement from the countries' foreign ministers."The Government of Israel’s actions in the West Bank are undermining the possibility of a two-State solution," the statement reads, adding that there have been "unprecedented levels of settler violence and settlement expansion.""Together, we are resolute: the two-state solution must be protected, and we will take action in pursuit of a just and lasting peace," it continued.It comes after the Israeli government last month opened up tenders for the construction of around 1,200 housing units in the West Bank, drawing widespread condemnation from the international community and human rights groups.The units, destined for the E1 settlement area, would further isolate East Jerusalem from the rest of the territory.In their statement on Tuesday, the 12 foreign ministers called the decision to publish tenders "unacceptable."British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney "have agreed on the need to take action to prevent further damage," the statement added.'Ethnic cleansing'Speaking to parliament on Tuesday, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband accused "settler terrorists" of "ethnic cleansing" in areas of the West Bank, saying that the Israeli government had often "turned a blind eye to this."He announced that the UK would also be bringing in an "import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories.""I do not believe the British people want us supporting the occupation by accepting products from settlements in our shops and supermarkets," he told MPs.In a post on X, Miliband's French counterpart, Jean-Noël Barrot, said Paris had taken the decision to enforce the sanctions as the West Bank was "on the brink of explosion.""Unchecked expansion of settlements in violation of international law, a surge in violence committed by extremist settlers against Palestinians, and acts of terror condemned by the Israeli authorities themselves," he wrote.Burnham later issued his own statement on Tuesday evening, calling the newly announced measures "carefully judged, targeted steps that are not aimed at the Israeli people, but at the unacceptable policies of the current Israeli government.""Before I became Prime Minister, I said our country’s response had been too slow and simply not good enough. That’s why I committed to changing the government’s approach," the UK leader added.Israel respondsIsraeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar on Tuesday ordered the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem in response to the moves taken by Westminster, as he hit out at Miliband's statement."The accusations made today by the foreign secretary in the British Parliament were outrageous lies," Sa'ar said.Israel has also announced that it will henceforth refuse entry to 12 British nationals.The list reportedly includes former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, his Your Party cofounder and MP for Coventry South Zarah Sultana, and Diane Abbott, the MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington.The West BankThe West Bank has been occupied by Israel since 1967 and has seen a surge in violence since the start of the war in Gaza, which broke out following the Hamas militant group's attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023.According to a report from the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, there were around 737,000 Israeli settlers in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, as of October 2024.Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law.

[Courtesy] These are peculiar times in which big countries watch themselves lose geopolitical power while small ones thrust themselves upwards at the expense of stagnant or declining countries. This phenomenon of states stagnating or declining while a few rise socio-economically and gain geopolitical leverage is clearest in Europe, where new powers overtake entrenched ones. While the stagnation or decline is self-inflicted and externally stimulated, the rise is meticulously orchestrated to take into account new realities and to avoid blunders. One European country thrusting itself upwards at high speed and seemingly jumping over others is Poland. It also shows growing interest in Africa, especially Kenya. The Polish, tracing their origins and identity as a people to between 966-1025 CE, have had a rough 1000-year history in an area whose geographical size kept changing with geopolitical times. Divided among the Germans, Russians, and Austrians, they were solidified in the 20th Century’s two big wars, first as beneficiaries of US President Woodrow Wilson’s dream of safeguarding future peace by promoting the doctrine of ‘self-determination’ and second as victims of big power dealings. Wilson, probably the first Cold Warrior, successfully countered Vladimir Lenin’s threat to spread anti-capitalist Bolshevism to Eastern Europe. His 1918 Fourteen Points address had two primary objectives: to undercut Lenin and persuade the Germans to stop fighting. He had used idealistic language to thwart realistic threats arising from Lenin’s communist idealism. Restored Poland was one of the consequences of what Arthur Link considered to be Wilson’s ‘higher realism’. Lenin’s Bolshevik success, despite Wilson’s counter-move, had a long-term influence on different peoples who dreamt of overthrowing imperialism. They included the Chinese and Vietnamese who adjusted Marxism-Leninism to suit their revolutionary realities. In addition, Kenyan political adventurer Jomo Kenyatta reportedly used to hang portraits of Lenin, Mahatma Gandhi, and Paul Robeson in his office at the Githunguri Teacher’s College, Kenya’s pre-Mau Mau anti-colonial hotbed. Kenyatta and Robeson, roommates in England, were co-actors in the movie ’Sanders of the River’. Roughly 18,000 Poles, after Adolf Hitler attacked Poland to launch World War II, found refuge through Mombasa, Kenya, to other places. Post World War II, Poland, through big power deals, was forced into the Soviet Communist orbit. It remained communist until the collapse of the Soviet Union, after which it joined such Western institutions as NATO and the EU. In less than 40 years, thereafter, Poland moved from a poverty-stricken communist appendage to the Soviets into the fastest-growing economy in Europe. It, in 2026, ranks the 20th largest economy in the world and the sixth in Europe. It dreams of possibly overtaking Germany, the top in Europe and third in the world, by expanding while others contract. How it achieved such success was a subject of discussion between visiting Polish Deputy Foreign Minister Wojciech Zajqczkowski and USIU academics led by Vice-Chancellor Mwenda Ntaragwi. Poland’s post-Cold War socio-economic success was due to five factors. First, it created a proper governance and political atmosphere for innovation and skills borrowing, especially from neighbouring Germany. Second, with many economies in the West suffering downturns, ‘Polish’ workers transferred skills to the new Poland. Third, it received a lot of capital infusion from the EU to uplift its economy once it became a member. Fourth, young Poles attended Western institutions to acquire appropriate pro-capitalist attitudes and skills that were necessary for transforming society. Fifth, being relatively ethnically homogeneous, Poland did not worry about the PITO (Penetration, Integration and Take-over) principle and thereby escaped the New Right Movement’s xenophobic excesses. With its growing strength as Europe’s new capitalist haven, Poland wants to branch out to other regions for investment and geopolitical leverage.
